title: Parallax Compatibility Case (m-case-format)
description: The case envelope, grouped as given / when / then. Identity and routing (`model`, `tags`, `lane`) plus the explicit `shape` discriminator and the optional `compileEligibility` declaration (present only to mark a case RUN-ONLY for the compile sweep) stay top-level; everything else is bucketed into `given` (ambient world-state before the action: `fixtures`, `apply`, `fault`), `when` (the action under test and how the client performs it: `objectQuery` | `writeSequence` | `scenario` | `coherence` | `concurrency` | `boundary` | `attempts` | `write`, plus context `uow` / `mutation` / `at` / `observedTxStart` / `observedValidStart` / `equivalentEncodings`), and `then` (everything the case asserts: `statements`, `referenceSql`, `rows`, `graph`, `tableState`, `affectedRows`, `errorClass`, `nativeCode`, `outcome`, `rejectedRule`, `roundTrips`, `tolerance`). Every SQL statement — golden or naive — is a `{sql, binds}` statement entry (`$defs/statementEntry`): its `sql` is a dialect-keyed map (`postgres` / `mariadb`) at golden locations (`then.statements`, per-step `statements`) and a plain string at naive locations (`given.apply`); `binds` is authored once per statement and defaults to `[]`. A case is one of nine shapes, named by the required top-level `shape`: a `read` case (a queryable `when.objectQuery`, asserting `then.rows` / `then.graph`); a `writeSequence` case (ordered DML under `when.writeSequence`, asserting `then.tableState`); a `scenario` case (m-unit-work — ordered steps under `when.scenario`, golden SQL per step); a `conflict` case (m-opt-lock — a single-attempt observation-requiring keyed write asserted by `then.affectedRows`, or an ordered `when.attempts` retry sequence); a `coherence` case (cross-process cache coherence — a two-node sequence under `when.coherence`); an `error` case (m-db-error — `then.errorClass` + `then.nativeCode`, triggered by top-level `then.statements` or a `when.concurrency` choreography); a `concurrencySuccess` case (m-read-lock behavioral read lock — a `when.concurrency` choreography with NO `then.errorClass`); a `boundary` case (m-auto-retry/m-opt-lock bounded automatic retry — `when.boundary` ordered actions + `then.outcome`, on the `api-conformance` lane, carrying no golden SQL); or a `rejected` case (m-value-object / m-predicate / m-object-query negative validation — a schema-valid `when.objectQuery` OR a `when.write` a model-aware validator MUST refuse PRE-SQL, naming the violated normative rule in `then.rejectedRule`, carrying no golden SQL). Every case carries an optional `lane` (`harness` default | `api-conformance`): a `harness`-lane case executes as today, while an `api-conformance`-lane case (every boundary case, plus the read-lock matrix reads) is schema-validated by the harness but satisfied by each language's API Conformance Suite.

oneOf.description: A read case: a queryable Object Query with expected rows or an expected object graph.
A writeSequence case: ordered DML asserted by the resulting table state (milestone-chaining temporal writes, batched non-temporal writes, m-detach detached insert/update merge-back).
A scenario case (m-unit-work): ordered operation steps with per-step round-trip counts proving the cache/identity contract. Golden SQL lives per step, so `then.statements` is absent.

A conflict case (m-opt-lock): an observation-requiring keyed write asserted by the number of rows it affects. Loads the model's fixtures, OPTIONALLY runs an out-of-band `given.apply` (a concurrent transaction's stale-version mutation or row removal), then runs the golden statement(s) and asserts the affected-row count. The written verb is `when.mutation` — `update` (the default) or `delete`; a temporal target's write is always the milestone close. Two forms: a SINGLE attempt (`when.write` + `then.affectedRows` + `then.statements`); or an ordered `when.attempts` retry sequence (each attempt carrying its own statements + affectedRows + write), proving the m-opt-lock retry contract — a stale UPDATE affects 0 rows, then a retry that re-reads the fresh version affects 1.

A coherence case (cross-process cache coherence): a two-node operation sequence under `when.coherence`, run against ONE database over TWO connections (node A, node B). Each step declares its node and golden SQL; the case asserts what node B observes after node A's committed write.

An error-classification case (m-db-error): triggers a real DB error and asserts the neutral category it classifies to (`then.errorClass`) plus the per-dialect native code (`then.nativeCode`). A case MUST declare a trigger: top-level `then.statements` (single-connection, uniqueViolation — ordered DML whose final statement raises) OR a `when.concurrency` choreography (two-connection, deadlock / lockWaitTimeout — barrier-separated rounds).

A concurrency-success case (m-read-lock behavioral read-lock): barrier-separated `when.concurrency` rounds on two held non-autocommit sessions asserting NO error is raised. Every PRESENT step declares an explicit `kind`: a read step (`kind: read`) carries `rows` it MUST return on its HELD session; a write step (`kind: write`) omits it and asserts only that it did not block/raise. The `not: then.errorClass` guard keeps the shape distinct from an error/concurrency case. The nested `rounds.items.properties.{A,B}.required: [kind]` forces a PRESENT success step to declare its kind structurally, without forcing A/B to exist.

A boundary case (m-auto-retry/m-opt-lock bounded automatic retry): a unit-of-work loop-mechanics case the single-connection harness cannot provoke. It carries `lane: api-conformance` and is satisfied by each language's API Conformance Suite; the harness schema-validates it but does not execute it. It declares the portable unit-of-work body (`when.boundary` ordered actions), the portable expected outcome (`then.outcome`), an OPTIONAL injected fault (`given.fault`), and its retry configuration under `when.uow`. It carries no golden SQL — `then.statements` is disallowed — and `lane` is REQUIRED and pinned to `api-conformance`.

A rejected case (m-value-object / m-predicate / m-inheritance / m-storage-layout negative validation, resolved Q7 + Q3): a model-aware validator MUST refuse the input BEFORE emitting any SQL, and `then.rejectedRule` names the violated normative rule. `when` carries EXACTLY ONE invalid input — an `objectQuery` (a SCHEMA-VALID m-object-query document, predicate included, that violates a resolver MUST or the m-value-object materialization/navigation contract), a `write` (a neutral write row whose value-object document is invalid, a predicate-selected instruction, or a whole KEYED instruction whose shape a model-aware validator refuses), OR a `model` (an inline descriptor whose accepted-model formation has a standalone/table-level defect or a cross-entity family-invariant defect). The inline `model` stays quarantined inside the case so the shared models registry remains loadable and is round-tripped through descriptor serde before semantic validation asserts the rejection. The `oneOf` below, paired with the `propertyNames` enum that forbids other keys, admits EXACTLY ONE of `objectQuery`/`write`/`model`. A rejected read names its own queried position inside its `objectQuery`, so no lane falls back to a default root. All three `write` forms are OBJECTS, which this branch requires: the shared `when.write` vocabulary also carries the multi-key ARRAY form, and that form is the conflict lane's alone — it states one collapsed statement's aggregate affected-row count, which a rejection asserted pre-SQL has nothing to say about. Admitting it here would leave the graders reading one input two ways, since a rejected case's dispatch asks which MEMBER a write carries and an array carries none. It carries NO golden SQL because rejection is asserted pre-SQL, on no dialect. Purely schema-level negatives stay schema-validation unit tests, not rejected cases.

allOf.description: A temporal optimistic close records `when.at` as the finite Transaction-Time close instant and requires `when.observedTxStart`, the observed Transaction-Time start (`in_z`) the optimistic gate binds. Every close is observation-backed in both modes; a locking-mode close omits only the GATE, so an `observedTxStart` standing alone is not merely unnecessary there but refused, while the `observedValidStart` + `observedTxStart` EDGE pair stays legal in both modes because it selects the milestone rather than gating on it.

A `when.write` that is a whole KEYED INSTRUCTION (`$defs/keyedWrite`, recognized by the `mutation` + `entity` + `rows` it carries together) belongs to the `rejected` shape alone. Every executing shape reaches its keyed instructions through `when.writeSequence` or a `when.scenario` step's own buffer, whose golden SQL is what grades them; the rejected lane emits no SQL, so it is the one lane where the instruction ITSELF — rather than a row's contents or a statement it produced — is the input under test. This tests the keyed instruction's WHOLE member set rather than `rows` alone: `rows` is reserved from `$defs/bareWriteRow` and so already cannot appear on a row, and keying this restriction on the same members that pick the branch keeps a malformed input reported as the branch mismatch it is instead of as a shape violation.

A scenario carrying a KEYED WRITE action step (`insert` / `update`) is `lane: api-conformance` throughout. What such a step observes is which verbs accept a live client-held VALUE of a stated provenance, which the wire harness can neither construct nor arrange, so it cannot execute the step at all — and a scenario is ONE ordered execution, not a set of steps to divide between executors. Assigning the whole case to the API Conformance Suite is therefore the only routing under which every step of it runs: a `harness` lane would report the case as run while the very step it turns on never executed.

A scenario carrying a KEYED WRITE action step carries ONLY keyed write action steps. Because such a case is `api-conformance` throughout, the API Conformance Suite is its ONLY executor — and that suite asserts no golden SQL (`m-api-conformance`), while a `scenario` asserts no `then.tableState` either. A neighbouring read / write / lifecycle step brings an oracle no one here can grade: the wire harness that owns golden SQL never runs the case, and the suite that runs it may not assert that SQL. Admitting the mixture would therefore admit a case gradeable neither whole nor in part, which is why the uniformity is a grammar rule rather than an executor's complaint.

`then.roundTrips` may declare ZERO only for the two shapes that can cost nothing: a `scenario`, whose total is the SUM of its steps' own counts and is therefore zero exactly when every step costs nothing (a keyed write action step observes a value's provenance and emits no statement either way), and a `rejected` case, which a validator refuses PRE-SQL and which therefore always costs zero. Every other shape asserts one operation that reaches the database — a read's golden SQL, a writeSequence's ordered DML, a conflict attempt, the statement an error case raises — so zero states an impossible total there and stays a schema violation rather than a later harness failure.

A `rejected` case declares the round trips it actually costs, and a pre-SQL refusal costs NONE: the validator refuses the input before any statement is composed, so `then.roundTrips` is pinned to `0` where it is declared at all rather than merely permitted to be. The property's own default of `1` describes the shapes that reach the database; this shape's effective default is `0`, the same number a declaration would carry, which is why every rejected case in the corpus omits it.

Which branch of `then.execution` a case may author is decided by its SHAPE, not chosen freely. A `read` case's whole observable is one read issued outside any unit of work, so its provenance is the Read Trace itself and it authors `readTrace`; every other executing shape runs inside a transaction boundary, whose provenance is the Execution Log spanning its attempts, so it authors `transactionLog`. Without this the closed union is closed over its own members only: a transactional case could author a bare `readTrace` — discarding the attempt, status, and retry-policy assertions that are the whole point of a transactional oracle — and a standalone read could author a log describing a boundary it never opened.

model.description: Path to the model descriptor, relative to core/compatibility/.

tags.description: Module/feature tags driving coverage and test selection.

lane.description: Which executor satisfies this case (m-case-format lane routing). `harness` (the default) — the m-case-format compatibility harness executes it as today (golden-SQL / data observables). `api-conformance` — a runtime-loop or read-lock-matrix branch a single-connection harness cannot provoke: the harness schema-validates it but does NOT execute it, and each language's API Conformance Suite MUST satisfy it. Every `boundary`-shape case is `api-conformance` by construction; the read-lock matrix reads (`m-read-lock-002`, `m-read-lock-004`, and `m-read-lock-005`) are `read`-shape `api-conformance` cases.

shape.description: The explicit case-shape discriminator: cases are self-describing, and the `oneOf` keys on this `const` for precise validation errors. The reference harness reads this field directly instead of sniffing which keys happen to be present. The schema still enforces shape-consistent required members (per branch), so a mislabeled case cannot validate.

compileEligibility.description: The compile-eligibility declaration (m-case-format / m-conformance-adapter). ABSENT by default: a case is compile-eligible, so an adapter's `compile` command emits its SQL statically. PRESENT only to declare a case RUN-ONLY — its emissions cannot be derived without executing SQL, so `compile` on it returns `status: run-only` with a `compile-run-only` diagnostic instead of `ok`, and only `run` grades it. Eligibility is an AUTHORED, REVIEWED intent declaration (intent is a human judgment); the harness mechanically backstops the detectable single-connection cases and each language's refusing compile port structurally enforces query-result dependence at runtime.

mode.description: The only declared mode is `run-only`: the field's presence declares the case ineligible for the compile sweep. A compile-eligible case simply omits `compileEligibility`.

reason.description: Which run-only criterion applies. `single-connection` — the case intends to exercise database concurrency or locking behavior (a `conflict` / `concurrencySuccess` / `boundary` shape, a `when.concurrency` choreography, or a `given.apply` / `given.fault`), so it is run-only regardless of whether its emissions happen to be statically derivable; the harness backstop requires this declaration on every such detectable case. `query-result-dependent` — the emissions are not a pure function of `when` + `given` (deep-fetch fan-out binds, materialized predicate writes, `sequence`-strategy PK allocations, framework-owned observed-version / `in_z` binds), so compiling would require executing a query; this criterion is a human judgment the harness cannot detect and each language's refusing compile port enforces structurally.

note.description: Optional human-readable justification for the reviewer.

given.description: Ambient world-state established BEFORE the action under test: the model fixtures to load, out-of-band SQL to apply verbatim, and any injected fault. Optional — a case that starts from the model's default fixtures and injects nothing omits `given` entirely.

fixtures.description: Whether the model's fixtures are loaded BEFORE the action — so a sequence can mutate pre-existing persisted rows (the m-detach detached-update merge-back case; the m-read-lock held-session reads). Defaults to false: a writeSequence case starts from an empty schema and builds its own state (the m-txtime-write milestone-chaining and m-batch-write batched-insert cases).

apply.description: conflict / temporal-conflict cases (m-opt-lock) only. An ordered list of out-of-band naive statement entries the harness applies verbatim AFTER the fixtures load and BEFORE the golden write, simulating a concurrent transaction that mutated or removed the row so the golden write reaches fewer rows than it addressed. Under `optimistic` mode the shortfall is a conflict the rendered gate detected; under `locking` mode the golden renders no gate and the same shortfall is a stale write. Each entry is a `{sql, binds}` statement whose `sql` is a plain string (dialect-agnostic naive SQL, run on every dialect). Absent for the success case (nothing intervened, so the write affects the row it addressed).

fault.description: boundary cases only. A portable fault kind injected at the database-port seam to drive the retry loop (aligned with the m-db-error `errorClass` vocabulary): a `serialization-failure` or `deadlock` transient (always retriable), a `lock-wait-timeout` (never retriable), or an `optimistic-lock-conflict` (retriable only under `when.uow.retryOptimisticConflicts`). Absent when the case exercises only loop configuration (`retries: 0`, the callback-withheld-on-abort case).

when.description: The action under test and how the client performs it. Exactly one action member is present per shape (`objectQuery` | `writeSequence` | `scenario` | `coherence` | `concurrency` | `boundary` | `attempts`, plus the single-attempt conflict's `write`); the context members (`uow`, `at`, `observedTxStart`, `observedValidStart`, `equivalentEncodings`) describe the unit-of-work mode, transaction instant, observed milestone coordinate, and alternate surface encodings.

uow.description: The unit-of-work configuration the action runs under (m-unit-work strategy selection + m-auto-retry/m-opt-lock bounded automatic retry). Optional and descriptive: it declares the resolved Concurrency Preference (so a case's mode-dependent golden SQL is self-describing) and the retry configuration a boundary case exercises. `locking` forces the effective Locking strategy for every lockable Entity. `optimistic` is the default and selects Optimistic for an Entity with an explicit-version or Transaction-Time-derived optimistic key, while an unversioned Non-Temporal Entity falls back to Locking. The target Entity's Effective Concurrency Strategy decides gate presence by itself, never the mutation kind: Optimistic omits the shared read lock and gates every observation-requiring write; Locking takes the qualifying shared read lock and emits no gate, though a versioned UPDATE still advances the version. The rule is uniform across the versioned keyed UPDATE, the versioned keyed DELETE, and the temporal milestone close. The harness executes the authored golden SQL either way; the block documents WHICH preference produced it.

concurrency.description: The Unit Work's Concurrency Preference: `optimistic` (default — a gate-capable Entity uses lock-free reads and observation-bound gates; an unversioned Non-Temporal Entity falls back to Locking) or `locking` (force shared-lock participation and ungated writes for every lockable Entity). Gate presence follows the target Entity's derived Effective Concurrency Strategy alone, uniformly across the versioned keyed UPDATE, the versioned keyed DELETE, and the temporal milestone close.

retries.description: The bound on automatic re-executions of the unit-of-work body after a retriable failure (m-auto-retry/m-opt-lock bounded automatic retry). Default 10; `0` disables the loop, so even a transient failure surfaces to the caller.

retryOptimisticConflicts.description: Whether an optimistic-lock conflict joins the retriable set for this unit of work (m-opt-lock). Default false — a conflict surfaces to the caller after one attempt. Transient database failures (deadlock / serialization failure) are always retriable regardless of this flag.

objectQuery.description: The canonical m-object-query document under test: one flat query naming its own queried `target` and carrying its `predicate`, `narrowTo`, `temporal`, `orderBy`, `limit`, and `includes` clauses as siblings. Present on read and rejected cases; absent on writeSequence cases. The `$ref` is the whole contract — no second hand-written pass validates it, and no envelope repeats the queried entity beside it.

model.description: rejected cases only (accepted-model formation, including m-inheritance / m-storage-layout, resolved Q3). An INLINE model descriptor document (an instance of metamodel.schema.json) carrying an accepted-model formation defect a model-aware semantic validator MUST reject before any SQL. This includes cross-entity inheritance-family invariants, a second independent owner of one structural Table, physical-column collisions within a uniquely owned Table, and rendered-key collisions that per-entity schema validation cannot express. Kept inline (never in the shared `models/` registry) so an invalid model cannot break sibling cases that load real models; round-tripped through descriptor serde before semantic validation asserts `then.rejectedRule`.

equivalentEncodings.description: Optional alternate authoring-surface encodings of the same Object Query (e.g. differently-ordered keys, an unsorted include set, or an omitted Transaction-Time selection). Each is a whole Object Query document and MUST normalize and canonicalize to `when.objectQuery`; the harness asserts this dialect-agnostically (layer 4c).

writeSequence.description: A writeSequence case: an ordered list of write steps the golden DML (`then.statements`) realizes. Each step names a mutation kind on an entity; the golden SQL is the matching ordered list of DML statements (one or more per step), applied in order, after which the harness asserts `then.tableState`. Used by milestone-chaining temporal writes (m-txtime-write), batched non-temporal writes (m-batch-write), detached merge-back delete (m-detach), and the minimal dependent cascade-delete witness (m-cascade-delete/m-unit-work).

allOf.description: A Bitemporal `*Until` step bounds a mutation to `[validFrom, until)` and records the Clock-supplied Transaction-Time instant in `at`.
A milestone-close `terminate` step carries the handle-supplied Transaction-Time instant in `at` for Transaction-Time-Only and Bitemporal entities.

An INSERT step's rows author no `observedVersion`: an insert opens a row rather than writing against one, so an observed version would name a milestone that does not yet exist (`m-unit-work` "Absence is structural" — the same rule `$defs/writeRow`'s own prose states as "absent on a versioned insert"). The shared `writeRow` definition cannot express it, because whether a row may carry the key depends on the mutation that owns it. This is the ONE arm of that rule the schema can decide: the other — a NON-VERSIONED target's row carries none either — needs the model. A `conflict` case's `when.write` and `when.attempts[].write` are the other two locations a case-format `writeRow` is authored, and neither needs this conditional: their verb is `when.mutation`, whose vocabulary is the keyed UPDATE and DELETE alone, so an insert is unrepresentable there.

mutation.description: The mutation kind. The `*Until` trio bounds a Bitemporal mutation to a Valid-Time window.

entity.description: The temporal entity the mutation targets.

statements.description: How many golden DML statements this step emits (for documentation / count consistency). The sum over all steps MUST equal the number of `then.statements` per dialect. This is an integer COUNT, not a statement-entry list (a writeSequence step carries no per-step SQL — the golden DML lives at `then.statements`).

rows.description: The neutral write input (①) for this step: the row(s) the mutation operates on, as flat attribute-named literals (`$defs/writeRow`). A GENERATING adapter classifies each field by metamodel role and derives the emitted column list + ORDER from the target's Entity Layout view, plus the SQL and the binds. `then.statements` stays an independent oracle the derivation cross-checks against. REQUIRED on every writeSequence step. A step on a TEMPORAL entity carries EXACTLY ONE row (`m-unit-work` "A temporal keyed instruction carries exactly one row") — each row chains its own milestones, so several rows are authored as several steps; the bound is model-dependent and so enforced against the metamodel rather than by `minItems`.

at.description: The Clock-supplied finite Transaction-Time instant recorded in `in_z`/`out_z`. It is execution context, not a durable write-instruction member, and is distinct from the Valid-Time `validFrom` bound.

until.description: The exclusive Valid-Time upper bound of a Bitemporal `*Until` write, paired with `validFrom`.

validFrom.description: The Valid-Time lower bound (`from_z`). Required by Bitemporal writes.

note.description: Optional human-readable description of the milestone-chaining effect.

scenario.description: A scenario (m-unit-work) case: an ordered list of steps proving the unit-of-work / identity / query-cache contract. A step is either a READ step (issues an `objectQuery`) or a WRITE step (commits DML via `write`). Golden SQL lives PER STEP (as `statements`), not at `then.statements`: each read costs a declared number of database round trips, and an interleaved committed write lets a later step prove read-your-own-writes or query-cache invalidation. The harness asserts the round-trip counts are internally consistent with the golden SQL each step lists.

oneOf.description: A read step: issues one Object Query. A cache miss costs >= 1 round trip and lists golden SQL; a cache hit costs 0 and lists none. It names its queried entity inside its own `objectQuery.target`, exactly as a read case does.

A write step: applies golden DML between finds. By default the DML is COMMITTED so a later find observes it; with `rollback: true` the DML is applied and then ROLLED BACK — UNGROUPED, that step's own unit of work; grouped (`uow`), the whole group's (see the sibling `uow` property). A no-op write issues NO DML: it declares `roundTrips: 0` and lists no `statements`. A GROUPED write MAY name the read step whose result it settles against with `on` (m-case-format *Settling against a grouped find*): the write then consumes the observation that read recorded, rather than one resolved from case state.

An ACTION step (m-case-format lifecycle vocabulary): performs a managed-object lifecycle verb named by `action` against the result of an earlier step (`on`). It carries per-step golden SQL (`statements`) when the verb hits the database (a `load` / `access` relationship query, a `flush` / `mergeBack` / `commit` DML) exactly as a read / write step does, and per-step observables: `expectRows` (rows a `load` returns or a re-read observes), `expectState` (the object's lifecycle state after the verb), `expectError` (a neutral application-lifecycle error the verb raises), and `sameObjectAs` / `differentObjectFrom` reference-identity assertions. A `load` / first `access` resolving read is INSTANCE-FORM (m-case-format *Read result form*, m-sql *Read projection*): it materializes the loaded / accessed related objects, so a value-object-bearing target projects its applicable Storage Layout `Document` slot, exactly as a deep-fetch child level does. A cache-hit re-access lists no golden SQL and declares `roundTrips: 0`, exactly like a cache-hit read step. Golden SQL still lives PER STEP, so a scenario case with action steps carries no top-level `then.statements`.

allOf.description: `set` is a MUTATE-only attribute-assignment map (the new attribute values a `mutate` action assigns). A step carrying `set` MUST be a `mutate` action step — `set` on a read / write step, or on a non-`mutate` action verb, is invalid.

A single step declares AT MOST ONE of `sameObjectAs` / `differentObjectFrom`: a step's identity relationship to one anchor is either sameness OR difference, never both (in particular, they can never point at the SAME step). Distinct identity anchors are expressed by separate steps or by the adapter's per-position identity checks (m-conformance-adapter).

An OBJECT-TARGETING action verb (`mutate` / `detachCopy` / `load` / `access` / `mergeBack`) acts on a PRIOR step's result, so it MUST name that source with `on`. The BOUNDARY / unit-of-work verbs (`flush` / `commit` / `abort`) operate on the unit of work as a whole rather than a specific prior object, so `on` is OPTIONAL for them (a `flush` MAY still carry `on` to document the buffered write it materializes). This is a per-verb conditional, NOT a blanket `on` requirement — a blanket rule would wrongly reject a legitimate boundary step.

A keyed write ACTION verb (`insert` / `update`) is handed a value rather than a prior step's result, so it REQUIRES the `value` provenance token and names no `on` (m-unit-work *Write value provenance*). `value` is legal on no other step: provenance is a property of the value a verb is handed, and every other step form is handed none. Such a step carries NO golden SQL and declares `roundTrips: 0` (m-case-format *Keyed write action steps*): a refusal stops the verb before it buffers anything, and the one acceptance this shape admits — the `update` of a value no author changed, per the sibling `insert` rule — buffers nothing either, so its whole observable is the per-step `expectError`.

An `insert` keyed write action step REQUIRES `expectError`. Such a step declares `roundTrips: 0` and carries no golden SQL, so the only ACCEPTED write it can express is one that MATERIALIZES NOTHING (`m-case-format` *Keyed write action steps*) — the `update` of a value no author changed, which buffers nothing. An accepted `insert` is never that: it opens a row, so the verb buffers a write the committing unit of work flushes, and the step emits DML. A step declaring acceptance (no `expectError`) beside that zero would assert two things that cannot both hold, and nothing could catch it: the wire harness never runs the case, the API Conformance Suite asserts no golden SQL, and it grades the zero as the absence of the very durable effect the acceptance produces. So an `insert` step states the refusal its value's provenance earns, and a keyed write whose acceptance is observable as an emitted statement is authored where that statement has an oracle, never here.
A scenario-step `referenceSql` is a naive oracle for a read (`objectQuery`) only; writes and lifecycle actions do not produce rows to compare.

`expectGraph` is legal ONLY on an `action: access` step (m-case-format *Relationship contents at a step*), and it names BOTH ends of the navigation it states: ONE materializing read (`on`) and the relationship it walked from that read's objects (`path`). A read-back step re-queries the database, so it proves the DATABASE is right and says nothing about the in-memory graph; only an access on a node the scenario already materialized proves the VIEW survived what the steps in between did. On a write step or any other action verb there is no navigated relationship for the contents to belong to. The `on` ARRAY form spans sources at DIFFERENT lowered coordinates, and contents assembled across several such views would be a graph no single materialized view holds — so an access stating contents names the single read whose Include Paths materialized them. `path` is required for the same reason the contents are keyed by that path's TARGET entity: the path-less `access` form resolves a query-backed list's own source entity and navigates NO relationship, so it has no relationship contents to state and no accessed path an `objectQuery.includes` could cover.

A step declares `expectRows` or `expectGraph`, never both. `expectRows` states the rows of the step's own source result while `expectGraph` states the contents of the relationship the step navigated TO, so the two would describe two DIFFERENT entities on one step. An author wanting the navigated entity's rows states them as `expectGraph` nodes.
A scenario-step `equivalentEncodings` list supplies alternate authoring forms of that step's canonical `objectQuery`, so it is legal only on a read step.

`uow` step-grouping is legal on a read or write step ONLY. An ACTION step (m-case-format lifecycle vocabulary) executes through the lifecycle-object engine path, which does not observe grouping, so `uow` on an action step is invalid.

A WRITE step's `on` names the read step whose result the write settles against (m-case-format *Settling against a grouped find*). The evidence a write consumes is transaction-scoped, so the reference is legal only on a step that declares `uow` — an ungrouped write shares no unit of work with any find and has nothing to settle against. It names ONE find, never an array: a keyed write settles against the one observed state the value it was handed came from, and a set of sources would name no single one. Every target profile is nameable — a milestone chain holds several rows per key, and a versioned Non-Temporal key holds one observed generation per read of it — and a write naming no find takes the group's latest reading of its key. It is legal only on the BUFFERED KEYED form (`write` as an array): a legacy string label carries no instruction for an observation to reach, and a predicate-selected write selects its own rows by predicate rather than consuming one milestone a find handed over — an `on` on either would name evidence nothing consumes.

objectQuery.description: The Object Query a READ step issues, naming its own queried `target`. Present on read steps; absent on write steps.

equivalentEncodings.description: Optional alternate authoring-surface encodings of this step's canonical `objectQuery`. Each normalizes and canonicalizes to it; in particular, an omitted Transaction-Time selection normalizes to explicit Latest.

write.description: Marks a WRITE step, in one of three forms (disjoint by JSON type). A legacy string LABEL (a coarse verb hint whose intent lives only in the golden SQL — a deferred migration, still carried by `m-identity-map-006/007/008/011`, `m-process-cache-003`, `m-detach-004`). A single predicate-selected `$defs/predicateWrite` instruction. Or a `$defs/bufferedWriteSequence` — the ORDERED buffer of one-or-more KEYED write instructions a single unit of work accumulates and flushes together (m-unit-work), so the step encodes every buffered mutation explicitly rather than in prose. The buffered form is a GENERAL ordered keyed buffer: it spans a single keyed write, a mixed multi-object flush (insert / update / delete of DIFFERENT objects), and the two-keyed same-object coalescing pair alike — same-object folding at flush is the runtime coalescing rule, not a structural constraint. Predicate-selected instructions inside a buffer stay deferred (keyed-only). Every structured form is the neutral requested operation the compile/run and API no-drift checks consume INDEPENDENTLY of golden SQL; golden SQL (`statements`) remains the independent expected lowering of the flush — for coalescing, one final-value write or NO DML — never the source an adapter deduces the writes from.

rollback.description: Optional (write steps only). When true, the step's golden DML is applied and then ROLLED BACK instead of committed — the observable form of the m-unit-work abort contract. UNGROUPED, this step's own unit of work rolls back right after it. Grouped (the sibling `uow` key), this declares the WHOLE group doomed: every step sharing the label stays inside the SAME held transaction, which rolls back after the group's LAST step (not necessarily this one) — so a later step in the same group (e.g. a find re-issued to force-flush a pending write) still observes the mid-transaction state before the abort erases it. The rolled-back DML still executes, so the step's roundTrips count its statements exactly as a committed write does.

uow.description: Optional per-step unit-of-work GROUPING label (m-unit-work; sibling of `objectQuery`/`write`/`roundTrips`, legal on a read or write step ONLY — the sibling `allOf` conditional forbids it on an action step, whose lifecycle-object engine path does not observe grouping). Steps sharing the SAME label execute inside ONE held transaction (one unit of work, one connection) instead of each step's own default boundary; steps carrying NO `uow` key keep today's semantics exactly (an ungrouped write step is its own commit/rollback boundary; an ungrouped find runs on the autocommit connection) — grouping is opt-in and changes the meaning of no existing (unlabeled) case. Steps execute in AUTHORED order; a group's own steps need NOT be contiguous — two groups MAY interleave (the classic optimistic-lock race: one unit of work's observing find, then a concurrent unit of work's observe-and-commit, then back to the first unit of work's own doomed write). The group COMMITS after its LAST step, UNLESS one of its write steps declares `rollback: true`, in which case the group ROLLS BACK after its last step instead — the whole group is the doomed unit of work, which is what lets a step later in the SAME group (e.g. a re-issued find) observe a force-flushed write the eventual abort then erases (`core/spec/m-unit-work.md` "Abort"). A read (`objectQuery`) step inside a group reads THROUGH the group's own transaction (read-your-own-writes): its `expectRows` are what THAT connection observes mid-transaction, not the post-commit / post-rollback state.

roundTrips.description: How many database round trips this step costs. A READ cache HIT costs 0; a read cache MISS that executes one statement costs 1. A WRITE step's round trips equal the committed DML statements it lists. MUST equal the number of golden SQL statements this step lists for each dialect.

statements.description: The golden SQL this step emits, as an ordered list of `{sql, binds}` statement entries (dialect-keyed map form). Present only for steps that hit the database (roundTrips >= 1); absent for a cache hit (roundTrips 0).

expectRows.description: The rows this step's find must return against the fixture data. A cache-hit step that reuses an earlier step's result MAY restate the same expected rows. `expectRows` is the observation channel for BOTH read lanes (m-case-format *Read result form*, m-sql *Read projection*): the form is fixed by the step's read semantics, not by this member — a managed-object find / refresh step, a relationship `load`, and a query-backed list's first `access` are INSTANCE-FORM (the object lane, projecting every applicable Storage Layout `Document` slot), while the internal materialized-predicate-write resolving find is ROW-FORM (the values lane, no instance constructed, omitting the `Document` slots by default and widening only where the write it serves needs one). Both project the same columns for a value-object-free target, so the lane adds no bind and changes no projection; the two value-object-bearing scenario witnesses are where they diverge — the subscriber witness keeps the default (a versioned resolve retains only the observed version, so it omits `address` where the managed find over the same row projects it), and the supplier witness widens it (a temporal resolve records a complete Predecessor Row, so it projects `address` even for a close that copies no payload).

expectGraph.description: The relationship contents an `action: access` step observes — the step-level analogue of `then.graph` exactly as `expectRows` is the step-level analogue of `then.rows` (m-case-format *Relationship contents at a step*). Same shape as `then.graph`: an entity-name-keyed map whose value is a list of nodes, EVERY key a DECLARED model member name and every leaf its canonical Wire Value (m-wire), a to-many member a list and a to-one member a single node or null. Keyed by the TARGET entity of the relationship the sibling `path` navigates to, under that entity's LOCAL name. Collection kinds compare exactly as `then.graph`'s do (entity collections as multisets, a `multiplicity: many` Value Object positionally), and an unattached slot is authored ABSENT rather than empty, because a key one side carries and the other does not is simply unequal. The step's `on` read MUST carry `objectQuery.includes` covering the accessed path: an access over a relationship no read included has no materialized contents to state.

referenceSql.description: A read step's independent naive SQL oracle. It has the same string-or-dialect-map shape as `then.referenceSql` and, like that oracle, is self-contained rather than reusing golden binds.

sameObjectAs.description: Zero-based index of an earlier scenario step whose result denotes the SAME logical object(s) as this step (the identity-cache contract: same primary key => same object). Legal on a read step or an action step (a `load` / `access` re-read denoting the same managed object as an earlier step).

differentObjectFrom.description: Zero-based index of an earlier scenario step whose result denotes a DISTINCT object from this step — the reference-INEQUALITY counterpart of `sameObjectAs` (m-identity-map: two finite coordinates in one milestone are distinct pinned views even when their row values are identical, so value equality cannot distinguish them). Graded as REFERENCE identity by each language's API Conformance Suite; the wire harness proves the accompanying SQL / rows and skips this observable.

action.description: Marks an ACTION step and names the managed-object lifecycle verb it performs (m-case-format lifecycle vocabulary). `mutate` — assign the attributes in `set` in memory (no SQL for a snapshot / detached object). `detachCopy` — take a detached deep copy of the target (m-detach). `load` — explicitly trigger a deferred relationship load (m-deep-fetch), the portable, mandatory load trigger; its resolving read is INSTANCE-FORM (m-sql *Read projection*), materializing the loaded objects and selecting applicable Storage Layout `Document` slots. `access` — read a relationship / query-backed list (m-op-list): the FIRST access resolves and materializes the list in one INSTANCE-FORM read, while a later access hits already-populated state with no SQL. `flush` — emit the unit of work's buffered DML. `mergeBack` — reconcile a detached copy with the store (m-detach). `commit` / `abort` — end the unit of work, committing or discarding it (m-unit-work / m-detach). `insert` / `update` — hand the keyed write verb of that name a VALUE whose provenance the sibling `value` states (m-unit-work *Write value provenance*): the step observes which verbs accept that value, so it names no prior step and carries no golden SQL.

on.description: The earlier scenario step(s) whose result this step operates on. A single zero-based index, or an array of indices when an ACTION spans sources at DIFFERENT lowered coordinates (a coordinate-grouped `load`, m-deep-fetch / m-identity-map). Every index MUST name an EARLIER step (the harness asserts `0 <= index < the current step's index`); the array form's indices MUST be UNIQUE (`uniqueItems`) — a source is referenced at most once. On an ACTION step it names the source object(s) the verb acts on: REQUIRED for object-targeting verbs and optional for boundary verbs (see the sibling `allOf`). On a GROUPED WRITE step it instead names the SOURCE FIND — the read whose result the write settles against, so the write consumes the observation that find recorded rather than one resolved from case state (m-case-format *Settling against a grouped find*); there the single-index form is the only legal one and the step MUST declare `uow`.

value.description: insert / update action only (enforced by the sibling `allOf`, which also REQUIRES it there). The PROVENANCE of the value the step hands its keyed write verb, as m-unit-work *Write value provenance* partitions it: `unmanaged` — no managed read produced the value; `thisSource` — a read through the very source this verb writes through produced it; `anotherSource` — a read through some OTHER framework-managed source produced it, the same store or not. The case states the provenance and never how to obtain it: how an implementation retains which source produced a value is its own affair, so the adapter arranges a value of the stated provenance through its own managed reads — a read through the source under test for `thisSource`, a read through a second framework-managed source it supplies for `anotherSource`, and no read at all for `unmanaged`.

set.description: mutate action only (enforced by the sibling `allOf`). The attribute assignments a `mutate` applies, as an attribute-name-keyed map of new values.

path.description: load / access action only. The relationship (or dotted multi-hop relationship path) the verb navigates from the target object — e.g. `items` or `items.statuses`.

expectState.description: The lifecycle state the target object is in after this step (m-detach five-state machine): `in-memory` (new, uninserted), `persisted` (DB-backed, interned), `deleted` (marked for delete), `detached` (deep copy / scope-ended), or `detached-deleted` (detached copy marked for delete). An adapter-delegated observable — graded by each language's API Conformance Suite via the m-conformance-adapter `stateChecks` observation, and skipped by the wire harness. Legal on a read step or an action step.

expectError.description: A neutral application-lifecycle error this step's verb must raise: `detached-relationship-load`; `transaction-time-pin-read-only` for a mutation through a finite Transaction-Time-pinned view; or one of the three write-value provenance refusals (m-unit-work), which partition a value's provenance — `write-value-not-stored` for an update handed a value no managed read produced, `write-value-already-stored` for an insert handed a value produced by a read through the very source it writes through, and `write-value-foreign-lifecycle` for a value produced through some other framework-managed source, the same store or not.

identityAttr.description: The result-column name carrying the primary-key identity, used to check `sameObjectAs`. Defaults to the queried entity's primary-key column.

note.description: Optional human-readable description of the step's role in the scenario.

coherence.description: A coherence (cross-process cache coherence) case: an ordered list of steps run against ONE database over TWO connections modeling two application servers (node A, node B). Each step names the node it runs on, the query or DML it issues, and its golden SQL (`statements`); a write step (kind `write`) COMMITS on its node, a read step (kind `read`) is a query. The final step is node B's re-fetch after node A's committed write — it carries `observeRows`, the post-write rows node B MUST observe.

allOf.description: A read step (`kind: read`) issues one `objectQuery`, which names its own queried entity in `target`, exactly as a read case does.

node.description: Which application-server node (which connection) this step runs on. `A` is the writer; `B` is the peer whose cache must converge on A's committed state.

kind.description: `read` issues a query (a seed read or a re-fetch); `write` issues DML that COMMITS on its node (the change a peer must observe).

objectQuery.description: The Object Query a `read` step issues, naming its own queried `target`. Present on read steps; absent on write steps.

statements.description: The golden SQL this step emits, as an ordered list of `{sql, binds}` statement entries (dialect-keyed map form). A read step's is a SELECT; a write step's is the committing DML.

observeRows.description: The rows this step MUST observe. On the final node-B re-fetch this is the POST-WRITE state (proving the cache converged on node A's committed write); on a seed read it is the pre-write state. A coherence re-fetch materializes / refreshes a managed object, so `observeRows` carries an INSTANCE-FORM read (the object lane; m-case-format *Read result form*, m-sql *Read projection*) — a value-object-bearing target would project its applicable Storage Layout `Document` slots here, though every coherence-read entity is value-object-free today.

sameObjectAs.description: Zero-based index of an earlier coherence step (on the SAME node) whose observed rows denote the SAME logical object(s) as this step — the identity-preservation contract: the cross-process refresh updates the interned object in place (same primary key => same object).

identityAttr.description: The result-column name carrying the primary-key identity, used to check `sameObjectAs`. Defaults to the model root entity's primary-key column.

note.description: Optional human-readable description of the step's role in the coherence scenario.

concurrency.description: The two-connection choreography for deadlock / lockWaitTimeout error cases and the concurrency-success read-lock cases. Ordered, barrier-separated rounds; each round names the statements nodes A and B run that round (a node absent from a round is idle). Each node step carries `statements` (dialect-keyed golden SQL entries), mirroring a coherence step. The runner runs each node on its own non-autocommit session, synchronizes rounds with a barrier, and (for an error case) classifies the error raised in the contention round.

boundary.description: boundary cases only (m-auto-retry/m-opt-lock bounded automatic retry). An ordered list of the actions the unit-of-work body performs, portably described so the case is self-documenting without carrying golden SQL. The m-case-format harness never executes these (the case is `api-conformance`-lane); each language's suite realizes them through its idiomatic public API.

action.description: The unit-of-work action this step performs, portably named (the concrete API is per-language). `join` opens a JOINED unit of work that shares the current one rather than a nested boundary of its own (m-unit-work), so every action after it runs inside that joined scope; the list stays FLAT because the body is one linear sequence, and what a case asserts about the sharing rides `then.outcome` and `then.execution` rather than the list's shape.

note.description: Optional human-readable description of the action's role in the loop scenario.

attempts.description: conflict cases (m-opt-lock), retry form. An ordered list of optimistic-lock UPDATE attempts applied (after any `given.apply`) in sequence, each asserting its own affected-row count — proving the m-opt-lock retry contract end-to-end: the first (stale-version) attempt affects 0 rows, then a retry that re-reads the now-fresh version and re-applies affects 1. When present, the single-attempt `then.statements` / `then.affectedRows` are absent and `then.tableState` (when authored) asserts the retried write landed.

statements.description: This attempt's golden write statement(s), as an ordered list of `{sql, binds}` entries (dialect-keyed map form).

write.description: This attempt's neutral write input (①): the flat attribute-named row (`$defs/writeRow`) the attempt operates on. For a VERSIONED conflict its reserved `observedVersion` is the version THIS attempt gates on; for a TEMPORAL close it carries the milestone pk (+, on a Bitemporal target, `validEnd` — the address's Valid-Time exclusive upper bound), with the close instant and observed gate in this attempt's `at` / `observedTxStart`. REQUIRED on every retry attempt.

at.description: conflict RETRY cases (m-opt-lock), temporal-close form. THIS attempt's close instant (→ the new `out_z` the milestone-closing UPDATE sets).

observedTxStart.description: This temporal-close attempt's observed Transaction-Time start (`in_z`), bound by the optimistic gate. A retry attempt names its close's ADDRESS directly and never the observed milestone's edge: the edge form (`when.observedValidStart`) selects among the case's own loaded fixtures, while a retry re-reads the state the concurrent `given.apply` writer left behind, so it is single-attempt only (m-case-format). This coordinate is therefore always the gate candidate, and a locking-mode close renders no gate, so authoring it requires `when.uow.concurrency: optimistic` — refused structurally above rather than ignored.

affectedRows.description: The rows this attempt's UPDATE must affect: 0 for the stale-version attempt (conflict), 1 for the fresh-version retry (success). Named to match the single-attempt `then.affectedRows` — no legacy `expected*` vocabulary survives in a migrated case body.

note.description: Optional human-readable description of this attempt's role in the retry sequence.

write.description: conflict cases, single-attempt form. The neutral write input (①) for this conflict's keyed UPDATE or DELETE (or a temporal / bitemporal close), as a flat attribute-named literal (`$defs/writeRow`): the primary-key attribute (classified to the `where` key), every assigned domain attribute (the `set` columns — none for a DELETE), and the reserved `observedVersion` control key. A TEMPORAL / Bitemporal close carries only the milestone pk (+, on a Bitemporal target, `validEnd` — the address's Valid-Time exclusive upper bound, which the close binds under BOTH Effective Concurrency Strategies and which may be finite or infinity); its close instant and observed gate ride in `when.at` / `when.observedTxStart`. Either way the golden statement + binds become an INDEPENDENT cross-check rather than a golden-parse tautology. An ORDERED ARRAY of rows is the MULTI-KEY form: one unit of work buffers every row and the batching rule collapses them into a single set-based statement whose one Key Target holds every key, so `then.affectedRows` is the AGGREGATE that complete target owns (m-batch-write; m-unit-work affected-row attribution). The array form is keyed and non-temporal — a versioned or temporal target materializes to per-row writes instead of collapsing. The `$defs/keyedWrite` branch is the `rejected` shape's alone (restricted below): a rejected case may pin a rule about the INSTRUCTION rather than about a row's contents, and only a whole keyed instruction — its `mutation`, its own `entity` handle, and its `rows` — can carry one. A reader dispatches the four branches on the members the input itself carries: `target` is the predicate-selected instruction, `rows` the keyed one, an array the multi-key conflict form, anything else the bare neutral write row (①), which names no entity handle and is therefore resolved against the model's default write root. The branches are DISJOINT because `$defs/bareWriteRow` — the single-row branch here — reserves `target` and `rows` from the row's own open vocabulary; each instruction branch is therefore load-bearing rather than shadowed by a row that would also admit it. Member dispatch answers for the three OBJECT branches alone, so the array branch is scoped to the shape whose affected-row aggregate it exists for: the `rejected` shape requires an object (restricted above), leaving no lane where an array reaches a reader that asks it for a member.

mutation.description: conflict cases (m-opt-lock), NON-temporal form. The keyed verb `when.write` names, defaulting to `update`. `delete` selects the versioned keyed DELETE instead, whose golden carries no `set` clause. The verb decides neither gate presence nor shortfall classification — the target Entity's Effective Concurrency Strategy, derived from `when.uow.concurrency` and its Optimistic Lock Facet, decides both uniformly for the versioned UPDATE, the versioned DELETE, and the temporal close. An effective-Locking golden renders no gate at all, so its zero-row outcome is the non-retriable stale write rather than an optimistic conflict. A TEMPORAL target ignores this field: its conflict write is always the milestone close.

at.description: conflict cases (m-opt-lock), temporal-close form. The close instant a TEMPORAL / bitemporal conflict close records under either Effective Concurrency Strategy — the new `out_z` the milestone-closing UPDATE sets on the one current milestone its address selects (the pk plus one exclusive upper bound per as-of axis). A GENERATING adapter DERIVES the close binds from it. Present on a temporal-conflict close; absent on a versioned conflict.

observedTxStart.description: The observed Transaction-Time start (`in_z`) used as a temporal optimistic-lock token. Alone, it is the ADDRESS form's gate candidate, so it requires `when.uow.concurrency: optimistic` — a locking-mode close renders no gate and would consume it nowhere, which is refused structurally above rather than ignored. Paired with `observedValidStart` it is instead the observed milestone's EDGE coordinate on the Transaction-Time axis, which selects the milestone in either mode, so the pair is legal under `locking` too. Never authored on the root `when` of a retry sequence: each attempt carries its own.

observedValidStart.description: The observed Valid-Time start (`from_z`) — the second half of the observed milestone's own EDGE coordinate, whose first half is `observedTxStart`. Authoring it names the milestone the close observed instead of naming the close's ADDRESS directly: the address's Valid-Time end and the optimistic gate are then both derived from the one milestone the coordinate selects, so a write's address and gate come from a single observation. An edge names every declared as-of axis, so `observedTxStart` is REQUIRED beside it (`dependentRequired` below); it is mutually exclusive with the write row's own `validEnd` (a case names either the observation or the address, never both, enforced below); and it is legal only on a Bitemporal target, whose key may hold several disjoint Valid-Time rectangles current at once — the target profile the schema cannot see, so the two implementations refuse it (m-case-format).

allOf.$comment: A close names the observed milestone or its address, never both (m-case-format).

A retry sequence's attempts each carry their own close and read their own coordinates, so an observation coordinate on the root `when` is consumed by no attempt. The two authoring locations are alternatives, never a default and an override (m-case-format).

A root `observedTxStart` without `observedValidStart` is the address form's optimistic gate candidate. Although `optimistic` is the runtime default, this gate-dependent case form requires the preference explicitly so its golden remains self-describing (m-case-format).
A retry attempt never names an edge, so its `observedTxStart` is always the gate candidate and needs the mode that renders a gate (m-case-format).

then.description: Everything the case asserts after the action runs: the golden SQL an implementation is expected to emit (`statements`), the naive oracle (`referenceSql`), the observed data (`rows` / `graph` / `tableState`), the counts and codes (`affectedRows` / `errorClass` / `nativeCode` / `roundTrips`), the portable boundary `outcome`, the execution-provenance `execution`, and the numeric-comparison `tolerance`.

statements.description: The golden SQL an implementation is expected to emit, as an ordered list of `{sql, binds}` statement entries. Each entry's `sql` is a dialect-keyed map (`postgres` / `mariadb`) and its `binds` are authored once (dialect-agnostic), defaulting to `[]`. For a deep-fetch read the list has one entry per relationship/deep-fetch level; for a writeSequence one entry per DML statement. The per-level binds for a deep-fetch child level are the distinct parent keys gathered from the previous level, which the harness asserts equal the authored binds.

rows.description: The rows the query must return against the fixture data (single-statement / flat-result cases). An ABSTRACT-target inheritance read (m-inheritance, resolved Q6) additionally carries a `familyVariant` key per row — the CONCRETE subtype name of that row, materialized from the tag metadata map (`tagValue` -> subtype name), NOT projected as SQL — alongside the full concrete-superset columns (non-applicable subtype columns are null). Row objects stay open, so `familyVariant` needs no separate schema property.

graph.description: The assembled object graph a read must produce. EVERY key is a DECLARED model member name — an Attribute by its own declared name, never its physical column — and every leaf is its canonical Wire Value (m-wire): UTC instants spelled with `Z`, decimals at declared scale, bytes as lowercase hex. For a deep fetch: the root rows, each carrying its eager-fetched related rows under the relationship name — OR, for a NARROWED polymorphic hop (m-deep-fetch, m-inheritance), under the DERIVED narrowed view key `<rel>[<Concrete>,<Concrete>]` (the local relationship name, the effective concrete-subtype set in canonical alphabetical order by entity name, no spaces; equivalent authored narrowings collapse to the same key). A polymorphic view's child objects additionally carry `familyVariant` (the concrete subtype name, materialized from the tag map, never projected as SQL). For a value-object materialization read (m-value-object): the owning entity's rows, each carrying its embedded value-object values decoded from the single structured-document column under the value-object name (a nested object for a `one` member, an ordered list for a `many` member, to arbitrary depth). Keyed by the root class's LOCAL name — result vocabulary, so it is derived by resolving the query's own `target` and taking the resolved Entity's local name rather than reusing the canonical spelling `target` carries — whose value is a list of root objects; a related set appears under its relationship name (or narrowed view key), and a value-object member under its declared name. The REQUESTED INCLUDE TREE bounds the value, not the identity graph: a relationship reaching an ancestor already on the current path (a BACK-REFERENCE cycle, m-snapshot-read) is unwound like any other level, so it renders its target once, in full, at the depth the tree still admits — and terminates because the tree strictly shrinks with depth. A diamond-shared node at a non-cyclic position likewise keeps its full-value representation. A result position whose stored state contradicted the model carries `null` here and states its diagnoses in `then.storedDataIssues`.

graphs.description: An ORDERED array of per-milestone snapshot graphs a `history` / `asOfRange` read materializes (m-snapshot-read, resolved Q5a), coexisting with the single-graph `then.graph` exactly as `then.rows` does: a single-instant read carries `graph`, a milestone-set read carries `graphs`. Each entry pairs a milestone `pin` — the EDGE coordinate this graph is pinned at, its OWN milestone's from-instant per as-of axis, NOT a shared root pin — with the assembled `graph` at that pin. So `history` returns one independently edge-pinned graph per milestone and `asOfRange` one per overlapping milestone (m-temporal-read edge-point reads). Each `graph` has the same root-class-keyed shape as `then.graph`.

pin.description: The milestone edge coordinate keyed by `valid-time` and/or `transaction-time`; each value is that milestone's own finite start instant.

graph.description: The assembled object graph at this milestone's pin — the same root-class-keyed shape as `then.graph`.

storedDataIssues.description: The stored-data diagnoses a read publishes for the result positions whose stored state contradicted the declared model (m-snapshot-read). One entry per INVALID position, in result order, so a conforming read authors none at all: `ordinal` is that position's zero-based place in the ordered result, `hydrated` states whether the normative collapse produced a value (the `then.graph` position carries it) or none could be produced without inventing one (the position carries `null`), and `issues` is the closed diagnosis set the position carries — deduplicated within the position and repeated across every position that reaches the same invalid node. Each issue names its closed `code`, the canonical `entity` the violation was found on, the dotted `member` path where one is nameable (absent for an unresolved family tag alone, whose discriminator is no declared member), and the affected `objectKey` where the object's own identity decoded.

tableState.description: The resulting table state a writeSequence or conflict case asserts after applying its ordered DML golden SQL. Keyed by table name; each value is the full set of rows that table must contain (order-insensitive). Row values speak DB column names; timestamp columns are authored as ISO-8601 UTC strings at core microsecond precision, with the open-bound `infinity` as the literal string `infinity`.

affectedRows.description: conflict cases, single-attempt form. The number of rows the golden write — a keyed UPDATE or DELETE, or a temporal milestone close — must affect after any `given.apply` is applied. The EXPECTATION it is graded against follows the write's TARGET, not whether optimistic locking applies: a Key Target expects exactly its key count (the AGGREGATE, for the multi-key `when.write` array form), a milestone close exactly 1. Meeting the expectation is success. A SHORTFALL is classified by the write's already-decided concurrency: a GATED (optimistic) shortfall is the retriable optimistic-lock conflict, an UNGATED (locking-mode) observation-requiring one the non-retriable stale write, and a shortfall on a target that required no observation at all (an UNVERSIONED keyed write) the non-retriable missing target — the rows addressed do not exist. An EXCESS over the expectation is invariant and never a concurrency outcome: it is always the non-retriable cardinality corruption, since no concurrent writer can make a correctly addressed target match more rows than it names. A case whose write is REFUSED commits no write effect, so it always asserts this count and its golden statement; an optional `then.tableState` observes the state that remains.

errorClass.description: error cases (m-db-error). The neutral m-db-error error category a triggered DB error MUST classify to. uniqueViolation = duplicate-key; deadlock = deadlock or serialization failure (retriable); lockWaitTimeout = blocked past the lock-wait budget.

nativeCode.description: error cases (m-db-error). The native code each dialect's driver MUST surface for this error, witnessing the divergence the classifier absorbs: Postgres a SQLSTATE string (e.g. "23505"), MariaDB a vendor errno (e.g. 1062). `errorClass` is the single dialect-neutral seam output; this is the per-dialect input.

outcome.description: boundary cases only. The portable expected outcome: `committed` (the unit of work eventually commits — the injected fault was auto-retried away), `aborted` (the closure threw and the boundary rolled back, withholding the callback's return value), or a surfaced error kind the caller observes (`optimistic-lock-conflict` when a conflict is not opted into retry; `deadlock` / `serialization-failure` / `lock-wait-timeout` when a transient exhausts the bound or the loop is disabled). The concrete per-language error type stays language-local; this is the neutral kind the suite asserts.

rejectedRule.description: The stable pre-SQL validation rule violated by a rejected case. The closed enum below is authoritative. Model-formation codes distinguish the fixed resolver's foundational Metamodel invariants, Inheritance-owned TPH/TPCS topology, root-owned temporal/persistence/optimistic facts and materialized-key collisions, and Storage Layout-owned independent Table-mapping and within-owner physical-column collisions; query and write codes retain declaration-owned member identity while validating effective applicability.

roundTrips.description: Declared number of SQL statements for the operation. For a deep-fetch read case this MUST equal the number of authored/executed `then.statements` for each dialect; child SQL is omitted when an earlier level gathers no parent keys. For a writeSequence case it MUST equal the number of ordered DML statements; for a scenario case it MUST equal the SUM of the steps' per-step roundTrips — which is ZERO for a scenario whose every step costs none (a keyed write action step observes a value's provenance and emits no statement either way). A `rejected` case costs zero too: its input is refused pre-SQL, so the top-level `allOf` pins it to 0 rather than merely admitting it. Those two shapes are the whole of the relaxation — the same `allOf` keeps the minimum of 1 everywhere else — and the default of 1 below describes the shapes that reach the database, so a consumer deriving an effective count for an undeclared `rejected` case reads ZERO rather than that default.

execution.description: The execution-provenance oracle (m-execution-log): what the run's Execution Log or Read Trace looks like. A CLOSED union of exactly one wrapper — `readTrace` for a case whose whole observable is one read, `transactionLog` for a transactional one — narrowed by the same `propertyNames` enum idiom the `when` branches use. Calls name their statement by INDEX into the case's flattened authored golden-statement order and never repeat SQL or binds: `then.statements` (and the per-step / per-attempt `statements`) stay the sole SQL and bind oracles, `then.roundTrips` the sole count oracle. Duration and the implementation-level error type name are omitted because neither is portable; they are checked against their general API contracts instead. This is a CASE ASSERTION FORMAT, not a public serialization contract, and the compatibility harness validates it without grading it — each language grades it through the conformance adapter's matching `execution` observation.

tolerance.description: Absolute tolerance for numeric row comparison. Omit for exact comparison (the default; money/counts/exact aggregates compare exactly in Decimal space). Declare ONLY for inherently inexact results (stddev/variance, repeating-decimal avg) that cannot be authored exactly and differ in scale across dialects; comparison then becomes abs(actual - expected) <= tolerance.

storedDataIssueCode.description: The closed public vocabulary of stored-data violations (m-snapshot-read). Each code names one violation a detecting seam judged without inventing a value; the first four collapse to a producible value and the rest leave the affected position unhydrated.

databaseCall.description: One ATTEMPTED database round trip (m-execution-log Database Call). `statement` is the zero-based index into the case's flattened authored golden-statement order — the call names the statement it ran rather than repeating its SQL or binds — and is OMITTED on a lane that authors no golden SQL (`api-conformance`), where `kind` and `completion` are the whole portable oracle. `kind` keeps a failed call classifiable without parsing SQL.

allOf.description: A `read` call admits Read Completed or Database Call Failed; a `write` call admits Write Completed or Database Call Failed. Keying the completion on the call's own kind is what makes the pair a closed algebra rather than two independent enums.

callCompletion.description: How a Database Call ended (m-execution-log), a CLOSED union of exactly one member. `readCompleted` carries the PHYSICAL row count the statement returned — never a count of result roots, unique graph nodes, or projection views. `writeCompleted` carries the affected-row count. `failed` carries the detached diagnostic's portable half alone: the neutral `m-db-error` category the failure classified to, `null` where it classified to none. The message, the native code, and the raised exception are not portable and are absent here.

readTrace.description: The calls one read issued (m-execution-log Read Trace). NON-EMPTY by invariant: a trace proves work that reached the database, and planning that fails before its first call creates no trace at all — the attempt's `failure` records that instead.

writeBatchTrace.description: The calls one flushed write batch issued (m-execution-log Write Batch Trace), naming the CLOSED `m-unit-work` trigger that produced it: `read-dependency` for the batch a dependent read forced — which appears immediately BEFORE the read trace it enabled — or `finalization` for the boundary-owned final batch. Non-empty by the same invariant as a read trace.

attemptTrace.description: One entry in a Transaction Attempt's ORDERED traces: exactly one `readTrace` or `writeBatch`, narrowed by the same `propertyNames` idiom the top-level union uses. The order is the order the work reached the database, which is what makes a dependency-triggered batch's position in front of its read an assertion rather than a convention.

attemptFailure.description: The DETACHED diagnostic a rolled-back Transaction Attempt retains (m-execution-log Attempt Failure). `phase` locates a failure that has no call at all — `body` (callback work, explicit reads, read-forced write batches), `finalization` (the boundary-owned final batch), `commit` (the durability boundary) — without exposing a stack location or an internal planner stage. `retryEligible` is the CLASSIFIER's verdict under the effective policy, independent of the remaining budget and claiming nothing about whether another attempt occurred. `databaseCall` is the zero-based index into THIS attempt's own flattened calls, present only where a failed port call or post-call enforcement of a completed one caused the failure. The error type name and message are implementation-level and absent here.

allOf.description: A `commit` failure references NO Database Call. The durability boundary is not a recorded call — begin, commit, and rollback count zero round trips and appear in no trace — so an index authored beside `phase: commit` can only name some earlier, unrelated statement.

transactionAttempt.description: One PHYSICAL attempt of the logical invocation (m-execution-log Transaction Attempt). `traces` is the ordered Read Traces and Write Batch Traces the attempt produced; it MAY be empty for an attempt that failed before reaching the database. `roundTrips` counts every attempted call, a failed one included, and excludes begin / commit / rollback. `status` omits the live `active` value the module's own algebra carries: this is a TERMINAL value graph, so every attempt it states has already transitioned. A `failure` belongs to a ROLLED-BACK attempt alone, which the conditional below states structurally.

allOf.description: Only a ROLLED-BACK attempt carries a failure. The diagnostic describes the attempt that rolled back, so authoring one beside `committed` states two outcomes for one attempt.

retryPolicy.description: The immutable effective Retry Policy the Execution Log retains once (m-execution-log / m-auto-retry), after defaults and outer-transaction inheritance resolve. It records the RESOLVED values only; whether the caller supplied one explicitly is not retained and has no authored spelling here.

transactionLog.description: The whole Execution Log of one logical transaction invocation (m-execution-log), spanning every physical attempt including a joined body's, which shares this log rather than opening a second one. `concurrency` is the resolved Concurrency Preference, not a claim that every Entity used one strategy; `retryPolicy` is likewise the resolved value retained once. `roundTrips` is the sum over the attempts.

entityName.description: A metamodel Entity spelling, bare or namespace-qualified (identity.schema.json) — the entity a write-sequence step mutates or a write instruction targets. The same grammar the Predicate schema's attribute/relationship references use before the member dot; a read names its queried entity inside its own Object Query.

referenceSql.description: Independent naive SQL oracle. Required for non-trivial reads and optional for trivial single-table predicates. A string is dialect-neutral; a dialect-keyed map MUST cover the exact golden SQL dialect set, which the harness verifies.

predicateWrite.description: A predicate-selected write over the canonical instruction shape. `validFrom` and `until` are Valid-Time bounds; `at` is Clock-supplied Transaction-Time context and is not a durable instruction member.

at.description: The Clock-supplied finite Transaction-Time instant for a temporal predicate write.

validFrom.description: The Valid-Time lower bound of a plain or bounded temporal operation.

until.description: The exclusive Valid-Time upper bound of a bounded operation (`thru_z`), paired with `validFrom`.

allOf.description: A bounded predicate write is over `[validFrom, until)`, so it must carry both Valid-Time bounds; unbounded forms must omit `until`.

keyedWrite.description: A keyed write inside a buffered scenario. `validFrom` and `until` are Valid-Time bounds; `at` is Clock-supplied Transaction-Time context. Flush-only observations are not durable row members.

rows.description: The buffered instruction's rows, the canonical durable shape (`write-instruction.schema.json#/$defs/writeRow`). An entry on a TEMPORAL entity carries EXACTLY ONE row (`m-unit-work` "A temporal keyed instruction carries exactly one row") — each row chains its own milestones, so several rows are authored as several buffer entries; the bound is model-dependent and so enforced against the metamodel rather than by `minItems`.

validFrom.description: The Valid-Time lower bound of a temporal keyed write (`from_z`).

until.description: The exclusive Valid-Time upper bound of a bounded keyed write (`thru_z`), paired with `validFrom`.

at.description: The Clock-supplied finite Transaction-Time instant this buffered write flushes at (`in_z`).

allOf.description: A bounded keyed write is over `[validFrom, until)`, so it must carry both Valid-Time bounds; a plain write must omit `until`.

bufferedWriteSequence.description: The ORDERED buffer a single unit of work accumulates and flushes together (m-unit-work) — one or more KEYED write instructions, in the order they were requested. This is a GENERAL ordered keyed buffer: entries MAY name different entities and different primary-key identities (a mixed-object flush — an insert of one object, an update of another, a delete of a third — such as `m-unit-work-009`), and a buffer MAY hold a single keyed instruction (a buffer of one — the single INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE writes). Same-object folding at flush IS the coalescing rule, and it is a RUNTIME / planner property, not a structural one: when two buffered entries name the SAME entity and primary-key identity the flush combines them (a same-transaction insert-then-update writes the final value in place with no intermediate milestone; insert-then-delete cancels to no DML). The two-keyed same-object insert-then-update / insert-then-delete pair is that rule's single-object SPECIAL CASE, not a separate shape — the three same-transaction coalescing witnesses (`m-txtime-write-008`, `m-bitemp-write-014`, `m-unit-work-010`) are exactly that pair. The step's golden SQL (`statements`) is the INDEPENDENT expected lowering of the flush (one final-value write, NO DML, or the ordered per-object statements of a mixed flush), so a scenario encodes every requested mutation here explicitly rather than in a prose note. Predicate-selected instructions are deliberately EXCLUDED (keyed-only): a predicate-selected buffered write is the one generality still deferred to the string-label→structured migration.

statementEntry.description: One logical statement in the execution sequence: a closed `{sql, binds}` object. `sql` is a plain string at naive locations (`given.apply`) or a dialect-keyed map (`postgres` / `mariadb`) at golden locations (`then.statements`, per-step `statements`); `binds` is authored once per statement (dialect-agnostic) and defaults to `[]`. The `{sql, binds}` wrapper keeps dialect keys and entry-level keys in separate namespaces, so the schema needs no reserved-key carve-outs.
